title: Explain the Chain of Responsibility design pattern (request passed along handlers) with an approval-escalation example.
shortTitle: Chain of Responsibility pattern: passing a request along a chain of handlers (approval-escalation example)
topicTitle: Behavioral: Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template
keyPoints: A request walks down a line of handlers, and the first one capable of handling it does so; the sender never picks the handler.
Each handler holds a reference to the next handler and decides whether to process or forward the request.
The sender is decoupled from the concrete receivers, so adding a new handler requires zero changes to existing ones.
Two variations exist: pure CoR where exactly one handler processes, and pipeline where every handler runs in sequence.
Spring Security's filter chain is a real production example of Chain of Responsibility.
A terminal handler must always exist to prevent requests from silently vanishing.

s1_definition.oneliner: A request walks down a line of handlers, and the first one capable of dealing with it does so: the sender never picks the handler.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Chain of Responsibility** – a behavioral pattern that passes a request along a chain of handler objects.
- **Handler** – an abstract class or interface declaring a method to handle the request and holding a reference to the next handler.
- **ConcreteHandler** – implements the handling logic and decides whether to process or forward.
- **Decoupling** – the sender has no idea which handler will ultimately process the request.
- **Extensibility** – adding a new handler is inserting a new link in the chain with zero changes to existing handlers.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh walks into National Bank of India and asks to approve a large transfer of twelve lakh rupees. The junior clerk can approve up to fifty thousand, so the clerk passes it to the branch officer who can approve up to five lakh. Still not enough, so the officer passes it to the branch manager who can approve up to twenty lakh. The manager approves it. Rajesh never had to know who would approve it: the request travelled up the chain until someone with enough authority handled it.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Transfer Request (INR 12,00,000)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  limit: 50,000
  │    Clerk      │──→ cannot handle
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ forwards
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  limit: 5,00,000
  │   Officer     │──→ cannot handle
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ forwards
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  limit: 20,00,000
  │   Manager     │──→ APPROVED
  └──────────────┘
```

```text
  Pipeline variant (validation)
  ─────────────────────────────
  Request ──→ AmountValidator ──→ KycValidator ──→ LimitValidator
              (check amount)      (check KYC)      (check limit)
              All must pass for the request to proceed
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Chain of Responsibility is a behavioral pattern where a request is passed along a chain of handler objects, and each handler either processes the request or forwards it to the next. The real power is decoupling: the sender does not need to know which handler will ultimately deal with it, which keeps the sender simple and makes the handler set easy to extend and reorder.

In the banking project at National Bank of India, Rajesh uses this pattern for transfer approval escalation. Different tiers: a clerk approves up to fifty thousand, an officer up to five lakh, and a manager up to twenty lakh. Instead of one giant if-else method, each tier is its own handler class. The teller submits the request to the first handler, and it travels up the chain until someone with enough authority approves it.

The benefit is clean extensibility. When the business adds a regional head tier for transfers above twenty lakh, Rajesh writes one new handler class and wires it at the end. No existing code is touched, which is the Open/Closed Principle. Each handler also has a single, clear responsibility, so the code is easy to test.

One production detail to always stress is the terminal case. If a request exceeds every handler's authority and there is no fallback, it can silently vanish, which is dangerous in finance. A real-world example of this pattern at framework level is the Spring Security filter chain, where each filter either handles the request or calls the chain to pass it forward.

Remember one sentence: Chain of Responsibility passes a request down a line of handlers, each processing or forwarding, so the sender is decoupled from the receivers and the chain is freely extensible.
